newsitem.title: UK: Governments condemn IRA murder of policemen.
newsitem.headline: Governments condemn IRA murder of policemen.

text.p: IRA guerrillas came under mounting international pressure to end hostilities in Northern Ireland on Tuesday after they killed two policemen in an ambush that threw hopes of a lasting peace into disarray.
The province's police chief said there was no sign of the IRA laying down its weapons and his officers were on alert in case of more attacks.
Police detained a man for questioning about the Irish Republican Army double murder that caused widespread revulsion and raised fears for the future of a shaky truce by pro-British Loyalist militias.
"One person has been arrested in relation to the murders. There is an ongoing investigation," said a spokeswoman for the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair renewed a charge that the killers who shot the officers at close range in the town of Lurgan on Monday had set out to sabotage an Anglo-Irish peace initiative.
U.S. President Bill Clinton castigated the IRA for "this brutal act of terrorism".
"There is nothing patriotic or heroic about these cowardly killings," said Clinton in a written statement issued on Monday night. He also warned against retaliation by pro-British Loyalists.
European Union leaders meeting in Amsterdam said they were horrified at the double murder. They reaffirmed "abhorrence of terrorist violence in all its forms".

Blair, whose condemnation has been backed by outgoing Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, accused Irish republicans of bad faith over a peace process that has been dogged by violence since the end of an IRA ceasefire in February 1996.

Britain broke off tentative contacts with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, immediately after the ambush. London and Dublin have insisted that the IRA call a ceasefire before they will invite Sinn Fein to talks.
Blair said in Amsterdam that the EU had taken the unusual step of issuing a unanimous statement about the atrocity because the guerrillas had made a "deliberate attempt to stop" the peace process.

"So it's not merely our repugnance at the killing and our deep sympathy for the families, it's that there is such a serious element of bad faith ...and I think the Americans, as everyone else has been, have been really shocked by this."

Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, said his party would continue to try and bring about "real and meaningful and inclusive peace negotiations" but agreed the killings had created a "very dangerous situation".
He declined to condemn the shootings during a BBC radio interview, but described them as a human tragedy. The IRA wants to unite the island of Ireland and British forces to leave Northern Ireland.

RUC chief Ronnie Flanagan was pessimistic about the immediate future. "All the indications we have lead us to believe that in the immediate future there is no prospect of a restoration of a cessation of violence," he warned.
Anxiety grew that banned Protestant Loyalist groups might attack Catholic nationalists.
The Combined Loyalist Military Command, the umbrella group for outlawed militias loyal to London whose October 1994 truce has been breached several times recently, stayed silent.
Gary McMichael, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party, the political arm of a banned Protestant guerrilla group, told Sky News that the way forward was through dialogue.
"This is the most critical point we have experienced in recent years and the IRA must recognise the implications of a continued conflict, and they must call an immediate ceasefire."
Politicians said that the IRA attack was designed to inflame sectarian tension during a "marching season" by Protestant Orangemen who loudly trumpet their allegiance to London.
More than 3,200 civilians, police, soldiers and guerrillas have been killed since 1969 in sectarian conflict between majority Protestants and minority Catholics in Northern Ireland.
